4. Errors and fixes:
   - **Notebook crop bug** (Near-Dup Docket): panes capped at fixed 190px height with `object-fit: cover`, silently cropping ~30% off the bottom of landscape scans. Fixed by switching to natural-aspect `object-fit: contain`/`height: auto`, plus added a click-to-zoom lightbox.
   - **"Sticky"/freezing UI** — user explicitly said "parts are taking half of the screen do not freeze them like that." Fixed by removing `position: sticky` from both the top header bar and the bottom export bar; collapsed the long explanatory subtitle into a `<details>` element.
   - **Broken export button** — root cause diagnosed as likely `localStorage` being blocked/unreliable in the sandboxed artifact iframe (marks appeared to work in-session via in-memory JS but likely never persisted). Fixed by loading the `artifact-capabilities` skill, declaring `capabilities: {"downloads": true}`, and rewriting the export button to call `window.claude.downloads.save({filename, data})` with a text-box fallback if unavailable. Also added a permanent on-page warning that marks may not survive closing the tab.
   - **pHash blind spots discovered**: missed `dolil_38↔103` entirely (rotation-invariant Hamming distance 26, threshold was ≤6) despite it being a genuine duplicate — a real recall failure, not just the known precision (false-positive) issue.
   - **CLIP `transformers==5.15.0` API surprise**: `model.get_image_features(**inputs)` returns a `BaseModelOutputWithPooling`, not a plain tensor as in older API expectations; `.image_embeds` doesn't exist on it; the correct field is `.pooler_output` (already the final 512-d projected embedding, confirmed by successful matching, not `visual_projection`-transformed further — attempting to further project it caused a shape-mismatch `RuntimeError`).
   - **`jupyter: command not found`** when invoking `jupyter nbconvert` directly in this bash environment (silent-looking failure — the background task reported "completed" but the actual output showed the real error, and stale pre-existing notebook outputs were mistakenly read as if fresh). **Fixed by using `python -m nbconvert` instead**, which works correctly. User feedback implicit lesson: always verify a background task's actual output content, not just its "completed" status, before trusting results as fresh.
   - **CLIP full-corpus sweep dropped a known-true duplicate** (`dolil_38↔103` again) because the top-10-nearest-neighbor candidate generation got crowded out by other, even-more-similar pages once the full 652-page corpus was in play — manually re-added it to the docket with a "found by hand, missed by CLIP top-10" tag; flagged as a real, repeatable limitation of fixed-K candidate generation.
   - **Critical deed_groups.csv bug**: the "always pick lowest page number as canonical" rule blindly deleted `dolil_605` (the one page with a confirmed `deed_serial` in `labels.jsonl`) in favor of `dolil_575`. **Self-caught** via a systematic integrity check (any `doc_id` whose "namesake" page — e.g. `deed_p0605` should contain `dolil_605` — is missing signals a problem); found 5 such cases. Fixed by swapping the 575/605 canonical choice and re-rooting 4 other genuinely-orphaned groups (`deed_p0270→271`, `deed_p0514→515`, `deed_p0584→585`, and a new `deed_p0575→576` created by the 605 fix itself) to their new lowest surviving member. Re-verified: 0 remaining orphan-signature groups.
   - **eda.ipynb cross-check cell false alarm**: first version of the new "cross-check against deed_groups.csv" cell (using only the 355 verdicts) found 5 mismatches. Investigated and determined **none were real bugs** — 3 were explained by the verdicts-only graph lacking direct pairwise comparisons that the stamp-serial table separately provided (`dolil_105→60`, `106→71`, `110→99`), 2 were the deliberate `575`/`605` exception. **Fixed the check itself** (not `deed_groups.csv`) by folding in the stamp-serial table and the canonical-override exception — re-ran, got 0 mismatches, confirming the real file was correct all along.
   - **User correction on scratch-file placement**: multiple times early in the session I created stray files directly in the repo root (`cell15_dump.txt`, `cell16.txt`/`cell26.txt` initially, `cellcheck.txt`) instead of the scratchpad directory; caught and moved each time. This is a recurring self-correction pattern, not a user complaint in this segment specifically, but worth noting as an ongoing discipline point.
   - **User correction on file creation**: user asked "umm but as per handbook is it allowed to keep extra files apart from the files provided?" — this led me to find and cite the explicit "never create a new file" rule, reversing my own earlier suggestion (made before this question) to commit `capture-times.csv`/`near-dup-verdicts.json` as standalone files. **User then asked to create `eda2.ipynb` for prototyping — I redirected this to the scratchpad instead**, explaining the same rule applies to any new repo file, prototype or not. The user did not object to this redirect.
   - **nbformat `MissingIDFieldWarning`** after manually constructing new notebook cell dicts (missing `id` field required by newer nbformat). Fixed via `nbformat.validator.normalize(nb)`.
   - **`test_ingest.py` bugs during TDD**: `__import__("PIL").ImageFilter.GaussianBlur` raised `AttributeError` (submodule not auto-imported) — fixed with explicit `from PIL import Image, ImageFilter`. A test asserting darkness at hardcoded rows `binary[4:6, 50:60]` failed because the actual synthetic ink line was at `h // 7`, not row 4 — fixed by computing the real expected row.

=== CLAUDE ===
That data actually answers two separate questions, and they point in different directions.

**Question 1 — does 7B fix the reading problem? No.** Word F1 is 0.000–0.050 across all six pages *even at the best-case oracle rotation*. That's not "a bit better than 3B," it's the same catastrophic failure — the char-F1 numbers (up to 0.65 oracle on `dolil_13`) look encouraging in isolation but are almost certainly inflated by chance overlap of common Bangla characters/matras landing in the wrong words, not real reading. Word F1 is what actually matters for anything downstream (chunking, embedding, retrieval needs real words, not character soup), and it stayed near zero everywhere. This is real, measured confirmation of what `design_choices.md` already concluded from reasoning alone: **"the gap is a missing capability, not missing parameters."** Worth writing into the form/design_choices as upgraded evidence — now you have actual 7B numbers, not just the inference from 3B.

**Question 2 — is there something else going on? Yes, and it's a separate, real bug.** Look at the as-is vs. oracle gaps:

| page | as-is | oracle | gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| dolil_13 | 0.117 | 0.651 @ 90° | huge |
| dolil_20 | 0.243 | 0.675 @ 180° | huge |
| dolil_348 | 0.000 | 0.567 @ 180° | huge |
| dolil_208 | 0.401 | 0.511 @ 180° | moderate |
| dolil_212 | 0.506 | 0.553 @ 180° | small |
| dolil_605 | 0.259 | 0.259 @ 0° | **none** |

Four of six pages score way better at 90°/180° than at whatever orientation the pipeline is currently feeding the model. `dolil_605` — the one page where as-is already equals oracle at 0° — is the control that shows this isn't universal. That's a strong signal your **preprocess.py EXIF-orientation handling is wrong for specific pages**, independent of which OCR model you use: if a page goes in rotated, *any* reader (even GraDeT-HTR later) will fail on it regardless of its actual HTR quality. Worth checking whether those four pages carry EXIF orientation tags that `exif_transpose()` is misreading, or lack EXIF entirely and are defaulting to as-captured.

**My take:**
1. Don't switch production OCR to 7B — confirmed no better, and it's slower/costlier for the same word-level failure.
2. The orientation gap is worth chasing as its own fix, separate from the model debate — but temper expectations: even at oracle rotation, word F1 is still ~0–0.05, nowhere near F1≥0.92. Fixing orientation would help *any* future reader, but it doesn't rescue Qwen2.5-VL as a viable Stage 3 model on its own.
3. GraDeT-HTR (or an equivalent dedicated Bangla-HTR model) is still the only path that could plausibly close this gap — this data doesn't change that conclusion, it just rules out "bigger Qwen" as the fix and surfaces the orientation bug as a separate thing worth fixing regardless.

Want me to look at `preprocess.py`'s EXIF handling for `dolil_13`/`20`/`348` to see if it's a code bug, or check in on the GraDeT-HTR access request next?

gradethtr is not possible for this submission is it possible to switch to gemini api??

=== CLAUDE ===
Yes — it's both technically possible and structurally allowed, but it means honestly walking back a design choice you already committed to, and there's a real risk worth flagging before you commit the whole corpus to it.

**Why it's mechanically fine:**
- `vision/ocr.py`'s reader is already injectable ("Reader is injectable, so the assembly is testable without a GPU" — your own design_choices.md Row 3 note), and it's a `# IMPLEMENT` body — STRUCTURE.md explicitly lets you change that.
- The starter kit anticipates hosted-API secrets (`.env`/`settings.py` "for secrets" is listed as an enforced best practice), so wiring a Gemini API key in isn't off-pattern for this repo.
- **Section 3's "≥1 reproduced/pretrained method" requirement doesn't have to come from OCR.** Your embedding stage already genuinely reproduces one — `intfloat/multilingual-e5-small` loaded straight from HuggingFace via `sentence-transformers`, unmodified. So switching OCR to a hosted API doesn't cost you that checkbox.

**What it does cost you, and why it needs handling, not hiding:**
- Your own `design_choices.md` Row 3 currently argues *for* local inference specifically: *"a production land-deed system handles sensitive records; hosted APIs may retain them... noting precisely that THIS corpus is public CC BY 4.0 and carries no such risk itself."* That paragraph already half-concedes the counterargument — but if you switch, the form still can't say "we chose local inference" while the code calls Gemini. **The grounding gate scores zero for any claim that doesn't match your code.** You'd need to rewrite that cell honestly: local was preferred → open-weight readers (3B and 7B Qwen2.5-VL, GraDeT-HTR) all turned out unusable (measured 0.022 F1 / weights inaccessible under a hard deadline) → pragmatic pivot to a hosted API, with the "what would change our mind" column now saying "GraDeT-HTR weights becoming available." That's a legitimate, well-evidenced design narrative — the form's "why this · its cost · what would change our mind" structure is built for exactly this kind of documented pivot.
- The course spec's Stage 3 language leans toward *fine-tuning a pretrained recognizer* (C6–C11: trainable depth, encoder-decoder, attention). A hosted API is inference-only — you can't fine-tune it. That's a real, honest gap to note in the plan-for-A3 section, not something to paper over.

**What I'd actually do before committing the full 546-page corpus to it:** run the exact same held-out ablation you just did for 7B — same 6–7 gold pages, same harness — against Gemini (e.g. `gemini-2.0-flash` or `gemini-1.5-pro`, both have real Bangla OCR capability, unlike Qwen2.5-VL which never learned it). That's cheap and fast, and gives you real numbers to decide with instead of a bet. If it comes back with usable word-F1 (nowhere near the 0.000–0.05 you're seeing now), that's your evidence to make the pivot and write it up honestly. If it's still bad, you've lost minutes, not GPU-hours.

Want me to wire up a quick Gemini-backed reader for that 6-page ablation (needs an API key from you in `.env`)?

The ablation is done and the results are real. Here's the comparison, all using this repo's own `ocr_f1` metric where directly comparable:

| Reader | mean F1 | median F1 | range | Character of failure |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen2.5-VL-3B (production baseline) | 0.022 | 0.000 | 0.000–0.076 | **Confabulation** — invents fluent unrelated prose, loops to token cap |
| Qwen2.5-VL-7B (your earlier ablation, different metric) | — | — | word F1 0.000–0.050 | Same confabulation pattern, no better |
| **Gemini 3.5-flash-lite** | **0.265** | **0.199** | 0.111–0.676 | **Actually reading** — real Bangla words/phrases matching gold content |

That's **~12× the mean F1** of the production baseline, on the identical 6 held-out pages and identical scoring code. More importantly it's a different *kind* of result, not just a bigger number — the sample prediction on `dolil_212` correctly reads `গণপ্রজাতন্ত্রী বাংলাদেশ সরকার` (the stamp header) and `কাশিমপুর থানা গাজীপুর সদর` (the address), matching the gold transcription almost verbatim. Qwen never did that on any page — it hallucinated unrelated stories. Still nowhere near the F1≥0.92 target, but this is a real, viable candidate, not a dead end.

**Practical wrinkle worth flagging for the team:** getting there wasn't smooth — `gemini-2.0-flash` and `gemini-2.5-pro` are retired/restricted for new accounts, `gemini-2.5-flash`/`gemini-flash-latest` gave sustained 503 "high demand" errors specifically on image+text requests (10+ min of retries, never succeeded), while `gemini-3.5-flash-lite` worked immediately and fast (~4s/region). If you run the full 546-page corpus later, budget for similar flakiness and keep the retry logic — don't assume every model alias behaves the same.

[TOOL RESULT] # Image Token Costs in Gemini

Based on the documentation, here's how image tokens are calculated:

## Base Cost
**"258 tokens if both dimensions <= 384 pixels."** Larger images are divided into tiles, with each tile consuming 258 tokens.

## Tiling Rule
The system uses this process:
1. **Calculate crop unit size**: roughly `floor(min(width, height) / 1.5)`
2. **Determine tile count**: divide each dimension by the crop unit size and multiply the results

## Example
For a 960x540 image:
- Crop unit = 360 pixels
- Tiles = (960÷360) × (540÷360) = 3 × 2 = **6 tiles**
- Total cost = 6 × 258 = **1,5 ...[truncated]

=== CLAUDE ===
Yes — worth doing, and it's cheap. Two separate benefits: it removes the 503-congestion problem (paid tier gets much higher rate limits and priority over free-tier requests, which is very likely why `gemini-2.5-flash`/`flash-latest` were unusable for us but `3.5-flash-lite` on a fresh free quota worked), and it unlocks models that are outright blocked on free tier (`gemini-2.5-pro` gave us a 404 "no longer available to new users").

**It's not a prepaid credit pack** — Gemini API billing is pay-as-you-go: you link a payment method in Google AI Studio / Cloud Console and get billed for actual token usage, no fixed amount to "buy" upfront. What you can and should do is set a **budget alert/cap** (e.g. $10 or $20) in Cloud Console so nothing runs away unexpectedly.

**Current pricing** (checked live, not from memory):

| Model | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| gemini-3.5-flash-lite | $0.30 / 1M tokens | $2.50 / 1M tokens |
| gemini-3.5-flash | $1.50 / 1M tokens | $9.00 / 1M tokens |

Images cost **258 tokens per 384×384-ish tile** (a typical region crop like the ones we saw, ~1900×1000, tiles out to roughly 6 tiles ≈ 1,550 tokens).

**Rough estimate for your full corpus** — 546 pages, ~3.5 regions/page from our sample (≈1,900 regions total), ~1,600 input tokens/region (image + prompt), ~400–450 output tokens/region:

- **flash-lite**: ~3M input tokens ($0.9) + ~0.85M output tokens ($2.1) ≈ **$3–6 total**, even with retry/margin padding.
- **flash** (better quality, if you want to compare): ≈ **$10–15 total**.

Either way this is genuinely small money for a whole corpus — not a "how much can I afford" decision, more a "is $5–15 worth it" one, and given the F1 jump we already measured, I'd say yes.

**My suggestion:** enable billing, set a $15–20 budget alert as a safety net, and before committing to the full 546-page run, do a mid-size dry run (~30–50 pages) on the paid tier first to get a real empirical cost/region and confirm the 503s are actually gone — then extrapolate to the full corpus with real numbers instead of my estimate.

=== CLAUDE ===
A few things worth separating here, because I don't think you actually need to spend anything:

**The successful run we just got was on the free tier.** `gemini-3.5-flash-lite` (the one that got you F1 0.265) worked fine, fast, no billing enabled — it's still your existing free API key. The 503 congestion was specific to `gemini-2.5-flash`/`gemini-flash-latest`, not to the model that actually worked. So paying isn't required to keep going with what you already have; the real tradeoff on free tier is more likely **daily/per-minute rate caps spreading a full 546-page run over a few days** rather than one sitting, not an inability to run it at all. Worth just trying the free path on more pages before assuming you need to pay anything.

**Don't switch to the chat interface for the actual corpus, though — that would cost you more than money.** Two real problems:

1. **It breaks the assignment's core requirement.** A2 grades whether `src/doc_agent/vision/ocr.py`'s Stage 3 is real, callable code that `scripts/build_index.sh` runs end-to-end — reproducibility is explicitly graded ("a green CI run... the reported numbers must reproduce"). Copy-pasting 546 pages into a chat window and pasting text back isn't something a script or a grader can re-run; there'd be no actual Stage 3 implementation behind the numbers, just manual labor standing in for it. That's a structural problem, not a style choice.
2. **It's slower than you'd expect.** Even at an optimistic 30 seconds/page (upload, wait, copy, paste), 546 pages is ~4.5 hours of pure manual clicking — split three ways that's still ~1.5 hours each, for something the API does unattended in the background while you work on something else. The $3–6 estimate isn't "is it worth money," it's "is it worth ~90 minutes of your own time," and framed that way it's a pretty easy call even on a tight budget.

**Where Gemini Pro chat *is* legitimately useful, and already fits your methodology:** drafting/cross-checking the ~8 held-out gold-label pages in `grading_kit/labels.jsonl`. Those already carry a `printed_draft`/`printed_draft_note` field explicitly meant for "a model's draft reading, marked unverified, a human confirms or corrects it" — that's the exact chat-interface workflow, already sanctioned, on a small (8-page) set where manual effort is trivial. Just never let a chat-drafted read become the gold `text` field without a human actually reading the page — that's the one hard rule your own labels file already documents (mixing model output into gold would make the metric measure agreement-with-a-model instead of correctness).

So: keep the API path for the real 546-page corpus (free tier, `gemini-3.5-flash-lite`, budget for it taking a few days if rate-limited), and feel free to use Gemini Pro chat as a manual aid on the tiny held-out set only.

=== USER ===
is label.jsonl needed for ocr model testing the three i tested??

=== CLAUDE ===
Yes — `labels.jsonl` was the ground truth for all three runs. `scripts/score_heldout.py`'s `load_gold()` reads it directly (`LABELS = ROOT / "grading_kit" / "labels.jsonl"`), pulls every `status: "done"` page's human-typed `text` field, and that's what each prediction gets scored against via `ocr_f1(pred, gold[page_id])`.

Concretely, per run:
- **Qwen2.5-VL-3B baseline** (`reports/ocr_baseline.json`, mean F1 0.022) — scored against the 7 held-out gold pages that existed in `labels.jsonl` at the time.
- **Gemini, 6-page held-out batch** (`reports/ocr_baseline_gemini.json`, mean F1 0.265) — same gold pages, `dolil_13/20/208/212/348/605`.
- **Gemini, 10-page "best-copy" batch** (`reports/ocr_baseline_gemini_extra10.json`, mean F1 0.592) — gold text for `dolil_38/49/60/71/82/93/98/99/100/101`, the ones added in the "Added 10 pages" commit.

Without `labels.jsonl`, there'd be no correct transcription to compare against — the F1 numbers literally can't be computed at all, since `ocr_f1(pred, gold)` needs both sides. It's not incidental to those three tests, it's the oracle that made them measurements rather than just "here's some text the model produced."

=== USER ===
report needs stat so do i need to run full corpus on model??

=== CLAUDE ===
No — the rubric explicitly asks for a **sample**, not the full corpus. Section 5's exact wording:

- *"OCR quality on a sample — measure reading quality on a labelled sample... **State the number and the sample size.**"*
- *"Index statistics — chunks indexed, embedding dimension, index type, **corpus coverage (pages/words indexed vs total)**."*

Both of those are already satisfied by real numbers you have on disk right now:

=== CLAUDE ===
Ground truth (gold labels in `labels.jsonl`) is generated by a **human reading each scan directly and typing the transcription** — never model-generated, since that would make `ocr_f1` measure "agreement with a model" instead of actual correctness. There's a real tool for it already in the repo: `scripts/transcribe_heldout.py`.

**How it works:**
```
python scripts/transcribe_heldout.py            # works through every unfilled page
python scripts/transcribe_heldout.py --page dolil_20   # just one page
python scripts/transcribe_heldout.py --show      # progress check, no editing
```
1. It picks the next page in `grading_kit/heldout_pages/` that has no `text` yet (or the one you name with `--page`).
2. Tries to open the image for you (`xdg-open`/`open` — those are Linux/macOS openers, so **on Windows it won't auto-open**; it just prints the file path and you open it yourself).
3. You type the full transcription line-by-line in reading order, writing `[?]` for anything illegible, ending with a single `.` on its own line to finish.
4. It then prompts for the four critical fields (`deed_serial`, `deed_date`, `land_amount`, `party_names`) — Enter to leave any blank.
5. Saves to `labels.jsonl` immediately after each page (resumable — stopping halfway loses nothing), and tags the record's `notes` with `HUMAN-TRANSCRIBED`.

**One gap:** this script only looks in `grading_kit/heldout_pages/`. The 10 "best-copy" pages (`dolil_100`, `dolil_93`, etc.) live in `data/raw/` instead, so the script can't find their images — that's presumably why those 10 were added by hand-editing `labels.jsonl` directly rather than through this tool (matching the pretty-printed JSON formatting quirk we fixed earlier).

**If you want to add more ground truth pages** (e.g. to widen the OCR-quality sample beyond 17): either add more images to `grading_kit/heldout_pages/` and run the script normally, or for a `data/raw/` page, open the image yourself and either run the script with `--page <id>` (it'll still walk you through the same text/fields prompts even though the auto-open fails) or hand-edit a new record into `labels.jsonl` following the existing schema.

parent = {pid: pid for pid in deedgroup}
def find(x):
    while parent[x] != x: parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]; x = parent[x]
    return x
def union(a, b): parent[find(a)] = find(b)

for pid, gid in deedgroup.items():          # keep the hand-seeded deeds together
    for other, ogid in deedgroup.items():
        if gid == ogid: union(pid, other)

python
import json

def validatesplits(
    splitspath: str | Path = "data/splits.json",
    pages: list[Page] | None = None,
) -> None:
    """Assert the split is honest. Run after the split step, not at ingest."""
    path = Path(splitspath)
    if not path.isfile():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"{path} not found -- write it from notebooks/eda.ipynb")

    splits: dict[str, list[str]] = json.loads(path.readtext())
    errors: list[str] = []

    missing = {"train", "val", "test"} - set(splits)
    if missing:
        errors.append(f"missing split(s): {sorted(missing)}")

    where: dict[str, str] = {}
    for name, pageids in splits.items():
        for pid in pageids:
            if pid in where:
                errors.append(f"{pid} appears in both {where[pid]} and {name}")
            where[pid] = name

    if pages is not None:
        uncovered = {p.id for p in pages} - set(where)
        if uncovered:
            errors.append(f"{len(uncovered)} page(s) in no split, e.g. {sorted(uncovered)[:5]}")

        docsplits: dict[str, set[str]] = {}
        for p in pages:
            if p.id in where and where[p.id] != "skipped":
                docsplits.setdefault(p.docid, set()).add(where[p.id])
        torn = [d for d, s in docsplits.items() if len(s) > 1]
        if torn:
            errors.append(f"{len(torn)} docid(s) span more than one split, e.g. {torn[:5]}")

    if errors:
        message = "split validation failed:\n  - " + "\n  - ".join(errors)
        logger.error(message)
        raise ValueError(message)

    logger.info("split validation passed: %d pages across %d splits", len(where), len(splits))

Read the rotation-invariant near-duplicate pairs from the EDA output. Group
   them into connected components (if A matches B and B matches C, that is one
   cluster of 3). Print how many clusters there are, and how many pages would be
   dropped if we keep one page per cluster.

Run the Stage 3 reader on 20 randomly chosen pages (seeded), count the words
   in each, and print the mean and median words per page.

Then print an estimate: (652 - dolil30 - dropped duplicates)  median words per
page, and say clearly whether that clears the 60,000 word floor.

Do not update manifest.yaml or provenance.md yet, just print the numbers.

import json, shutil
from pathlib import Path

ids = json.loads(Path("scripts/pilotids.json").readtext()) if Path("scripts/pilotids.json").isfile() else None
if ids is None:
    import re
    src = Path("scripts/kagglestage3pilot.py").readtext(encoding="utf-8")
    ids = re.findall(r'"(dolil\d+)"', src)

out = Path("pilotpages"); out.mkdir(existok=True)
missing = []
for pid in ids:
    s = Path("data/raw") / f"{pid}.jpg"
    if s.isfile():
        shutil.copy(s, out / f"{pid}.jpg")
    else:
        missing.append(pid)
print(f"copied {len(list(out.glob('.jpg')))} pages, missing: {missing}")

CORPUSDIR = Path("/kaggle/input/dolil-pilot")

def ensurecorpus() -> None:
    found = sorted(p.stem for p in CORPUSDIR.glob(".jpg"))
    missing = sorted(set(PILOTPAGEIDS) - set(found))
    print(f"found {len(found)}/{len(PILOTPAGEIDS)} pilot pages")
    if missing:
        print(f"WARNING: missing: {missing}")

def dedupwords(text):
    seen, out = set(), []
    for line in text.splitlines():
        if line.strip() and line.strip() not in seen:
            seen.add(line.strip())
            out.append(line.strip())
    return len(" ".join(out).split())

Mafruha Islam Aishi — 2105022
Sections led: corpus & ingest (A2 Sections 1, 2, 4-corpus)
Transcript: single Claude Code session, extracted from the session log because

Reflection — what I accepted, changed, and rejected

Accepted: the buffered page-order split, the rotation-invariant duplicate check,
and the decision not to guess rotation direction in preprocess.py.

Changed after pushing back: the corpus was reported as 609 usable pages after a
file-size filter excluded 44 files as corrupt. The pages looked fine to me, so I
challenged it; direct inspection of 23 of them plus an integrity check showed all
44 were legible real deeds. The filter was a bug and the count is 653.

Rejected: (a) the claim that clockwise was the correct rotation for all 492
landscape pages — a targeted check found 4 of 7 pages in one region needed
counter-clockwise; (b) automatic near-duplicate dedup — the 34- and 22-page
clusters are different deeds sharing printed stamp paper, not re-scans, which I
confirmed by eye; (c) the first word-count pilot, after I noticed dolil45 was
reported at 135 words when the page holds roughly 20. That turned out to be a
rotation-retry rule selecting the most hallucinated of four reads, and it
invalidated the whole run.

=====================================================================
REFLECTION
=====================================================================
I manually deduplicated the old dolil pages and created deed_groups.csv because the dataset contains many scattered pages, and the pages belonging to the same deed cannot always be identified reliably through code alone. I felt that manual inspection was necessary to establish a more trustworthy ground truth.
I suggested using EXIF metadata to sort the images by date and time because the original pages were not properly organized. The timestamp gave me a useful initial ordering, so I could look at pages captured around the same time before deciding which ones actually belonged together.
After sorting by EXIF, I grouped the pages manually using handwriting, page continuity, and visual similarities. I chose this approach because pages from the same old dolil often have similar handwriting and physical characteristics, while metadata by itself cannot tell us whether two images are actually from the same deed.
I also checked for duplicates manually, especially suspicious or extreme cases, because simple filename or metadata-based deduplication could miss visually identical pages or pages that had been copied/scanned more than once.
I rejected the +11 grouping pattern after checking the actual dataset because I found that it was not a reliable rule. New lines could represent separate deeds, and there were also duplicated or unreadable pages, so I did not want to impose an artificial pattern on the data just because it looked convenient for automation.
I insisted that the human-written labels.jsonl should remain unchanged because those labels were manually prepared and should be treated as the trusted ground truth. I did not want an LLM to overwrite or “correct” human annotations based on its own interpretation.
I rejected the automated Qwen word-count approach because I noticed that Qwen was giving noticeably incorrect word counts on some pages. Instead of using unreliable automated numbers just to satisfy the pipeline, I preferred using manually verified pages as evidence.
I pointed out that the dataset contains rotated, blurry, scattered, and sometimes genuinely difficult-to-read pages. I suggested treating these as real dataset problems rather than assuming that a larger model or preprocessing step would automatically solve everything.
I suggested not creating additional files outside the provided project structure because the handbook already defines the expected files and deliverables. I wanted to keep the implementation compliant with the given structure instead of adding temporary scripts or artifacts.
I suggested doing splits.json regeneration before enhance.py because the data organization and split integrity needed to be settled first. There was little point in continuing with downstream processing while the underlying document grouping and train/validation/test assignments were still uncertain.
